summary:
Gibraltar is a self-governing territory with its own Parliament and its own Supreme Court, which between them make and interpret its civil and criminal law. Measures enacted by the United Kingdom do not apply here of their own force: the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued in 2025 bind Gibraltar only if extended by Order in Council, and no such extension appears in the sourced material.

The principal legal gap for a trans visitor is gender recognition. No process exists in Gibraltar for changing a legal gender marker, and the sourced material records that transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore travels on a document whose marker cannot be altered by any local route, and can expect to be read in public and at the border under that marker.

Statutory discrimination protection covering gender reassignment, alongside sexual orientation, has been in place since 2007.

The Crimes Act 2011 was amended by a bill passed by Parliament on 19 September 2013, given royal assent on 25 September and in force from 10 October 2013, creating hate-crime and hate-speech offences on grounds of sexual orientation. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill amending those hate-crime and hate-speech provisions to include transgender identity, extending the same machinery to a trans person who is targeted for being trans.

In July 2026 Parliament also passed a bill making it an offence to offer or to practise conversion therapy.

Same-sex marriage has been lawful since a bill passed unanimously in December 2016 amending the Civil Marriage Act, and civil partnerships have been available since 2014, so a visitor travelling with a same-sex partner can expect that relationship to be legally recognised.

The sourced material contains nothing on document checks, entry screening, bathroom or facility access, or healthcare access for trans visitors in Gibraltar, and no incidents of violence against transgender people are recorded in it.
tangentialFactors:
Gibraltar's legislative moves on relationship recognition followed a public consultation launched in December 2015 that left Gibraltarians polarised, with an inter-ministerial committee chaired by a government minister weighing all viewpoints before the draft Civil Marriage Act amendment went to Parliament in August 2016; the main parties and the popular consultation indicated support for the change.

Official responses to hostility have been stated in anti-LGB rather than trans-specific terms. In July 2021 the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would 'urgently' consider legislation to tackle 'disgusting lurking homophobia' after an incident of anti-gay abuse, and Chief Minister Fabian Picardo used the same phrase about social-media abuse during Pride month; in the same month the Justice Ministry began investigating a proposal to make denigration of a person on the basis of sexual orientation a specific criminal offence. Nothing in that episode concerns transgender identity.

The United Kingdom's House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee, in its Seventh Report of 2007-08 on Overseas Territories, set accountability and good-governance expectations applicable to Gibraltar as an overseas territory, and its 2008 enquiry recommended that discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status be made illegal in all overseas territories. That recommendation is not law in Gibraltar; the local Parliament legislated for itself instead, first for sexual orientation in 2013 and for transgender identity in 2026.

The pattern across the sourced material is that protections framed around sexual orientation preceded trans-specific ones by roughly thirteen years, so a visitor should read the 2026 amendments as the point at which transgender status entered Gibraltar's hate-crime and hate-speech framework rather than as an established, long-tested regime.
localsOnly:
The Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, de jure legalising LGBT adoption, after a long-term lesbian couple denied adoption for want of legal recognition of their relationship challenged the law; Parliament then amended the law through the 2014 civil partnership legislation. The Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024 and explicitly allows same-sex couples to adopt children without discrimination.

In February 2021 Gibraltar enacted a surrogacy law permitting non-commercial, altruistic surrogacy for married couples or civil partners unable to conceive, with automatic recognition of children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination. In June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority approved an amendment to its in vitro fertilisation policy allowing lesbian couples to access assisted reproductive technology.

Age of consent for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender stands at 16. The Supreme Court ruled on 8 April 2011 that the then-higher age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set an equal age of consent of 16 that took effect on 23 November 2012. Before that, gay male minors faced a discriminatory age of 18, and a private member's bill to equalise consent was defeated in Parliament on 18 May 2009. Consensual relations between men have been legal since 1993, and equal age of consent followed in 2012.
